Unlike generic application software—which primarily focuses on user interface design, transactional clicks, and front-end user flows [1, 2]—the business requirements package for an **enterprise data platform** must specify the complex mechanics of data ingestion, movement, transformation, quality, storage, and governance [3, 4]. 

A well-formed data-platform requirements package consists of **six specialized, data-centric components**. The table below outlines these core components and details what distinguishes a robust, well-executed version from a weak, placeholder-level attempt:

---

### 1. Business Drivers & Analytical Workload Profiling
This component establishes the strategic "why" of the platform, aligning technical capabilities with business goals and classifying the exact analytical workloads the platform must support (e.g., Reporting/OLAP, Data Mining/ML, or Streaming) [5-7].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Anchors the data platform directly to measurable business outcomes or company OKRs (e.g., "reduce average time spent on weekly account preparation by at least 30%") [8, 9]. It profiles workloads by capturing explicit non-functional targets, including required latency (e.g., near-real-time vs. weekly batch), target user concurrency (high for BI, low for data science), and expected access patterns [8, 10].
*   **A Weak Version:** Relies on vague, non-testable placeholders (e.g., "The platform must be fast, scalable, and enable modern AI capabilities") or chooses a complex paradigm (like a decentralized data mesh or semantic fabric) without documenting the organizational readiness, staffing, or workload-driven justification to support it [10-13].

### 2. Upstream Data Source Inventory & Caveats
This section catalogs the target "data universe" by profiling where raw data originates, how it behaves, and how it will be transported into the system [8, 14].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Maps source system origins (e.g., application DBs, external vendors, APIs, local file shares) [8, 15]. It explicitly catalogs **data caveats**—such as seasonality affecting data volume, data skew, late-arriving data anomalies, and potential schema drift over time—enabling engineers to write defensive pipeline logic [8, 16].
*   **A Well-Executed Version also:** Outlines any static transformations that must occur during transport (such as decomposing compound fields, standardized unit conversions for dates/heights/weights, and handling null values) [17-19].
*   **A Weak Version:** Simply lists upstream system names (e.g., "EMR system, LSAH system") without documenting integration connection methods (ODBC, JDBC, SFTP), data modalities (structured, semi-structured, unstructured), or known upstream data hazards [8, 15, 17, 20].

### 3. Semantic Mapping & Business Glossary
This component provides the business context and meaning of the data fields, transforming raw, technical datasets into understandable business assets [8, 12].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Separates physical database column names from their real-world business meanings, providing a standardized Business Glossary and Data Dictionary [12]. For advanced architectures, it establishes semantic relationships and metadata schemas (mapping raw fields to enterprise-wide ontologies or global knowledge graphs) to enable conceptual search and discovery [21-23].
*   **A Weak Version:** Lacks standard definitions, forcing downstream users to guess what raw columns represent or leaving metadata as an afterthought. This quickly turns the platform into an unusable, fragmented **"data swamp"** [24-26].

### 4. Data Quality (QA) & Ingestion Validation Rules
To prevent a "garbage-in, garbage-out" effect, this component defines the automated tests and logical rules the platform must execute to verify data integrity [27, 28].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Establishes isolated, testable validation checks on ingestion (e.g., "numeric fields cannot differ by more than x% across consecutive data pulls") [8]. It defines clear operational metrics for monitoring (completeness, validity, accuracy, consensus) [27] and assigns specific business roles—such as **Data Stewards**—to manage data exceptions, error logs, and profiling jobs [29, 30].
*   **A Weak Version:** Uses generic requirements (e.g., "Data must be clean and accurate") without defining specific numeric threshold checks or logical rules, leaving data testing to be handled manually or by end-users after reports fail [27, 31].

### 5. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) & Persona Access Patterns
This component details the platform's security boundaries, defining who can access what data and the precise methods of consumption [32, 33].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Maps distinct user personas (e.g., Data Scientists vs. Business Analysts) to their preferred access patterns (e.g., direct SQL, REST APIs, interactive dashboards, or direct read access on raw cloud storage) [8, 34]. It specifies **fine-grained security rules**, detailing column-level permissions (projections), row-level permissions (filtering), and necessary data masking to protect sensitive data (such as medical PII or HIPAA-regulated information) [35-37].
*   **A Weak Version:** Specifies flat, monolithic access rules (e.g., "Finance has access to the database") without configuring row/column-level protections, resulting in security vulnerabilities or completely choking user utility by locking down entire tables unnecessarily [35, 37].

### 6. Storage Tiering & Data Lifecycle Management
This component dictates how data is physically and logically organized as it progresses from raw ingestion to retirement, directly impacting storage costs and compliance [33, 38].
*   **A Well-Executed Version:** Integrates a structured, zone-based landing architecture (e.g., transient landing, raw immutable, trusted, refined, and exploratory sandbox zones) [39, 40]. It defines explicit business criteria and timelines for moving data through its lifecycle phases (creation, storage, sharing, archiving, and secure destruction) [35, 38].
*   **A Weak Version:** Ignores storage architecture layers, treating the platform as a flat "dumping ground" for files, which leads to high cloud infrastructure costs, slow query performance, and severe regulatory compliance risks [25, 35, 41].

For a definition we follow Blohm et al. [ 19 ] once more: Definition 6. [ Data Mesh] “ Data mesh is a socio-technical, decentralized, distributed concept for enterprise data management [ 20 ] . It is characterized by the four principles of data-as-a-product, domain orientation, self-service platforms, and federated computational governance [ 32 ] .” Figure ˜ 8 illustrates the data mesh architecture. Van der Werf et al. [ 135 ] identify four archetypes, out of which the fine-grained fully federated mesh or short pure data mesh is considered to be the most theoretical and decentralized but also the most mature version. We have chosen this pure form in which individual nodes directly exchange data products and deliberately left out a central distribution layer. Every atomic team or business unit is responsible for a single domain and the data products arising from it. While this approach provides high flexibility and strong domain specialization, it might also introduce challenges such as wasting resources, when data transformations are performed redundantly due to lack of communication or transparency between domains. Here, the maturity of the self-service capability and federated governance components are particularly relevant. In the figure, one node is enlarged representatively to display more details. In each domain heterogeneous raw data emerges that will be stored in a data storage and operations platform of choice. Those can be whatever is available and suitable in the specific domain, e.g. data warehouse/lake, cloud storages or file storages etc. Each domain is responsible for transforming and packaging raw data into data products. Data products are further subdivided into data assets and raw data as inspired by Eichler et al. [ 43 ] . In each domain, data consumers and providers have access to self-service capabilities. In the figure, the individual nodes inherit self-service capabilities from a data fabric to represent the close relationship and potential synergy between the two paradigms. They are extended by domain-specific services as well as data product management where domain teams register their data products along with associated metadata, quality metrics, and access policies and facilitate the distribution to other domains. This data product management and distribution is overseen by a central data federated governance layer to enforce global governance standards consistently ensuring policies, interoperability and secure data access.

[ Semantic data lake] Semantic data lakes are a specific form of traditional data lakes that extend the capabilities through a semantic layer that enriches and connects the stored data semantically. The semantic layer equips data sets in the lake with connections from the data set's metadata to conceptual/logical models, which encapsulate knowledge potentially external to the content of the data, such as domain knowledge.

3.5 Data Fabric The concept of data fabrics was coined by NetApp in a white paper from 2016 as a “vision for data management […] that seamlessly connects different clouds, whether they are private, public, or hybrid environments” [ 62 ] . Back then, the term meant a combination of different data storage and integration techniques, however, without details about a concrete architecture. In 2019, Gartner defines a data fabric as a design concept for attaining reusable and augmented data integration services, data pipelines and semantics for flexible and integrated data delivery [ 29 ] . Hence, a data fabric is a technical architecture that brings together heterogeneous data that spans across multiple data sources; it allows organizations to monitor and manage data regardless of the location, considering appropriate data governance and data cataloging [ 20 , 83 , 2 ] . Then in 2021, Gartner [ 132 ] redefines a data fabric as a “design concept that serves as an integrated layer (fabric) of data and connecting processes”. In their data fabric architecture, Gartner emphasizes key characteristics, such as the use of AI for metadata management and data cataloging as well as knowledge graphs and ontologies to connect and enrich data sources with business related concepts. They introduce the notion of “passive vs active metadata”, i.e., data models, schema definitions, glossary, various logs are considered as passive metadata, whereas the continuous analysis of data usage with are described as active metadata describing actual experiences. The conversion of passive metadata into active metadata is interpreted as automating the collection and management of metadata [ 29 ] . By now, major vendors in data science have embraced the term; both vendors of semantic technology (e.g., Franz Inc., Ontotext, Pool Party, Stardog, and Top Quadrant) as well as more traditional vendors such as Microsoft, Oracle and Tibco [ 29 ] .

In 2014, Gartner [ 48 ] raised several criticisms of data lakes, warning that the indiscriminate ingestion of disparate data could lead to a so-called data swamp, making the data unusable without proper metadata management and governance [ 111 ] . Further, concerns included insufficient attention to data security and privacy oversight. In response to these critiques, Dixon revisited the data lake concept [ 39 ] . With Hadoop at the core, a key requirement was that a data lake should offer low-cost, easily accessible storage that supports a schema-on-read approach, meaning the metadata can be populated over time and transformations to apply the schema are only performed once required. This approach allows a data lake to automatically extract metadata from raw data and identify patterns, with users contributing additional descriptive information, such as domain-specific knowledge and attribute linkages. Hence, the idea is that the interaction between users and the data lake continually enhances (meta)data quality and value.

Fragmented Data Silos Across Business Units Large organizations' business data is likely to go back years or decades, scattered across multiple jurisdictions, business units, and departments, with disparate standards and formats, creating significant data silos. The presence of data silos is one of the main challenges for effective enterprise data management, standing in the way of creating a single source of truth. This is where the importance of data integration is particularly felt. When data is siloed, decision-makers can't rely on it due to inconsistencies or incompleteness, while reporting and analytics tools may return inaccurate outputs.

What are the most common enterprise data management failures? The most common EDM failures include poor data quality, unclear ownership, weak governance, fragmented systems, and the treatment of data management as a technology project rather than a business initiative. Many organizations also struggle because they focus on tools before establishing data standards, governance processes, and business objectives. As a result, data remains inconsistent, difficult to trust, and underutilized across the organization.

Key Components of Enterprise Data Management Data Quality Management Data quality management encompasses practices, processes, and tools for ensuring your data remains accurate, complete, reliable, consistent, and timely. It can include: Data profiling to map existing data and its structure and evaluate its quality Automated data cleansing and standardization to prevent errors and ensure data usability and reliability Data deduplication, merge, and survivorship rules Validation checks to verify data quality Data quality metrics monitoring (e.g., consensus, relevance, validity) Regular data quality audits and optimization.

Lack of proper data quality management poses risk management challenges, including the “garbage in, garbage out” effect. Your analytics and BI tools won't produce accurate results if the underlying data is incomplete or full of errors. It can also entail compliance risks, operational inefficiencies, and subpar customer and employee experiences. Data Security Management Any business deals with some amount of sensitive data. Failing to protect it may lead to data breaches and regulatory fines, which in turn cause reputational and financial losses. An average data breach costs businesses $4.4 million worldwide.

Client Integration Libraries This are Client integration Libraries that mostly cater for easy migration to Record Service. Using Record Service with Sentry provides these key benefits: Fine-grained security enforcement: Record Service enforces column-level permissions (projections), row-level permissions (filtering), and data masking across the IMPALA reservoir components. Performance:  Record Service is designed to be on the main data access path, meaning it needs to process every byte of data. Record Service scales horizontally to be able to run on the largest Hadoop clusters and high efficiency. It uses the Apache Impala IO layer, which utilizes low-level optimizations such as HDFS short-circuit reads and dynamic code generation to improve thread throughput and reduce CPU utilization. Record Service brings these performance benefits to the other components in Hadoop and accelerates their performance, despite adding a new layer in the stack. Simplicity: Record Service provides a higher level, logical abstraction for data. Datasets can be specified as logical names (i.e. tables or views) and Record Service returns schemed objects (in contrast to the storage APIs that deal with paths and bytes). This means that applications built on top of the Record Service APIs do not need to worry about differences in file formats, the underlying storage APIs, and other low level details.

When done right, data lifecycle management will help you maintain consistent data quality levels and reduce archiving, backup, and storage costs by removing data when it becomes obsolete. The data lifecycle consists of five phases: Creation : Collecting relevant data from its sources (IoT devices, forms, etc.) Storage : Transforming and adding data to storage Sharing and usage : Making the data available to business and external users with appropriate data access controls Archival : Keeping copies of data that's no longer needed for day-to-day operations Destruction : Securely purging data from archives.

Azzabi et al. [ 14 ] outline how the initial mono-zone architecture had notable limitations and hence data pond and zone-based architectures were introduced. Zone-based architectures include transient landing, raw, trusted, and refined zones, along with a sandbox zone for exploratory analysis. Each zone has a specific function based on its refinement level, from raw data ingestion and preliminary processing to serving compliant, quality-checked data to end-users [ 125 , 101 , 114 , 88 , 142 , 54 ] . A four-layered data lake architecture was proposed in [ 75 ] and is shown in fig. ˜ 5 . It resembles some ideas of zone-based architectures, such as a raw data 'zone' at the storage layer, and refined data in data marts at the transformation layer. In addition, it emphasizes the role of metadata and quality management on each of the layers.
